planting.note: Direct sow in fall into consistently wet soil or shallow standing water at a pond or wetland margin; water parsnip needs a cold winter stratification period to germinate well.

directions: Plant at a pond, ditch, or wetland margin in full sun to part shade, in consistently wet to saturated soil or shallow standing water. Water parsnip is a classic emergent wildflower of prairie pothole wetland margins, bearing flat white compound umbels from July through September atop tall stems that make it one of the best native pollinator magnets for small native bees, wasps, and soldier beetles, with occasional swallowtail butterflies nectaring as well. It spreads readily by seed in congenial wet sites, so give it room at the water's edge where that colonizing habit is welcome. Note that it closely resembles poisonous water hemlock (Cicuta) and should be positively identified before any foraging use.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into wet-mesic to wet soil in full sun to part shade; bluejoint grass forms a sod-forming matrix well suited to wet meadow restoration.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in wet-mesic to wet soil; bluejoint grass is a cool-season, sod-forming grass that dominates the wet meadow matrix of prairie pothole wetlands across the northern Great Plains, bearing airy purplish-green panicles in early summer. It provides strong erosion control at wetland margins and serves as a larval host for several skipper butterflies. Once established it spreads readily by rhizome to form a dense, self-sustaining stand, making it a good anchor species for a wet meadow or rain garden restoration planting.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into standing water or saturated soil at a pond or wetland edge; American mannagrass grows as a shallow-water emergent, not a dry-ground planting.

directions: Plant in full sun in standing water to saturated soil at a pond, ditch, or wetland margin; American mannagrass is a robust emergent grass with open, nodding panicles from June through August, forming the shallow-water fringe zone typical of prairie pothole wetlands. It provides valuable forage for waterfowl and muskrat, making it a good choice for a wildlife-focused pond or wetland restoration planting. Once established at the correct water depth it spreads steadily by rhizome and needs no further care beyond occasional thinning if it becomes too dense.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into consistently moist soil in full sun to part shade; streambank groundsel favors the moister western fringe of the prairie pothole region.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in consistently moist soil along a streambank, pond margin, or wet meadow; streambank groundsel bears cheerful yellow daisy-form flowers on upright stems from May through July, providing good early-season nectar for bees and small butterflies. It is native to the moister western fringe of the prairie pothole region extending into the Missouri Plateau, and performs best where soil moisture stays reliable through the growing season. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions or sow seed into pond margins or shallow standing water in spring; water smartweed grows as a floating-to-emergent aquatic and is not suited to ordinary garden soil.

directions: Plant in full sun at a pond or pothole margin in shallow standing water; water smartweed is a floating-to-emergent perennial bearing showy pink bottlebrush flower spikes from July through September, making it one of the best late-season nectar sources among prairie pothole aquatic plants and an important food source for waterfowl. It spreads by both seed and creeping rhizome across the water surface and mud margin, so give it room to colonize or contain it in a planted aquatic basket if a pond is small. It tolerates both floating growth in deeper water and rooted emergent growth in shallow mud.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into wet soil in full sun to part shade; Sartwell's sedge spreads by rhizome to form dense colonies at a wet-prairie or pothole edge.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in wet soil at a wet-prairie or pothole margin; Sartwell's sedge is a fine-textured, strongly rhizomatous sedge forming dense colonies at the water's edge, with an inconspicuous May-to-June bloom that matters less than its structural and wildlife value. It serves as a larval host for several satyrid and skipper butterflies and provides good erosion control along wet margins. Once established it spreads steadily to form a weed-suppressing colony, making it a useful utility planting for a wetland restoration or rain garden edge.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into saturated to shallowly flooded soil in full sun; awned sedge is a robust marsh-zone species for a pond or wetland restoration planting.

directions: Plant in full sun in saturated to shallowly flooded soil at a pond or wetland margin; awned sedge is a robust, coarse sedge dominant in the deeper-marsh zone of prairie pothole wetlands, with inconspicuous May-to-June flowers that give way to its real value as critical wildlife habitat. Muskrats build lodges from its dense growth and waterfowl use it heavily for nesting cover, while several skipper butterflies rely on it as a larval host. It spreads by rhizome to form extensive colonies once established at the correct water depth, making it best suited to a larger wetland restoration rather than a small garden pond.
